title: Evaluation of YouTube videos as sources of information about complex regional pain syndrome
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study. 167 English YouTube videos on complex regional pain syndrome (searched 5 May 2021) were scored on the Global Quality Score, the JAMA Benchmark Criteria and the Modified DISCERN Questionnaire. No video was ever judged true or false against an external ground truth: GQS rates flow and comprehensiveness, JAMA rates authorship/attribution/disclosure/currency, DISCERN rates sourcing. A wholly accurate video can score 'low content quality' simply for covering little, so under the instructions' QUALITY-vs-CONTENT test these are QUALITY scores, not misinformation prevalence. Screened INCLUDE only so that the QUALITY row is retained per §3 ('row kept, excluded from prevalence'); the paper contributes nothing to the prevalence estimates and would equally be defensible as a QUALITY-ONLY exclusion under §1.

estimates.country: Videos uploaded from the United States (80.2%), United Kingdom, India and others; analysis conducted in Turkey
estimates.measure_type: % of CRPS YouTube videos rated low content quality (Global Quality Score of 1 or 2)
estimates.denominator: 167 English-language YouTube videos about complex regional pain syndrome, from the first 300 relevance-ranked results, after exclusions
estimates.definition: Video scored 1 or 2 on the 5-point Global Quality Score, i.e. poor quality/poor flow with most information missing, or generally poor with information of limited use to patients
estimates.misinfo_def: since there is no mechanism for controlling the videos' contents and determining their accuracy, patients may access false information
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three researchers (physical medicine and rehabilitation, chronic pain) rated each video with GQS, JAMA and Modified DISCERN; inter-rater concordance was low (0.227 GQS, 0.206 JAMA, 0.037 DISCERN) and consensus was reached by discussion for discrepant items
estimates.moderator_quote: On May 5th, 2021, videos were searched using the keyword 'complex regional pain syndrome ' on YouTube. Relevance-based sequencing was used to sort the videos.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence. The GQS is a comprehensiveness/flow scale, so a factually accurate but brief video can be scored low; the paper never codes any video as false or misleading. Rank-truncated corpus (first 15 pages, 300 videos screened), hence denom_selection=curated. classification_level coded source_level because the instruments judge the video/resource as a whole rather than individual claims.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the other GQS cells (intermediate 37.7%, high 37.1%), the JAMA cells (insufficient data 29.3%, partially sufficient 69.5%, completely sufficient 1.2%) and the six Modified DISCERN cells — same quality instruments, further cells of the same distributions; one representative QUALITY row is enough since none of them measures falsity; (b) medians for GQS (3), JAMA (2) and DISCERN (2) — scale medians, not shares; (c) source, country and image-quality descriptives, correlations and group comparisons, all unrelated to misinformation prevalence. Worth a human's attention: the inter-rater concordance coefficients are very low (0.037 for DISCERN), and the authors handle this by consensus rather than reporting reliability after adjudication.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Keyword 'complex regional pain syndrome' searched 5 May 2021, relevance sort, 672 results, first 300 screened, 133 excluded (non-English, no audio, irrelevant, duplicate, advertisement, no CRPS information), 167 analysed. All three researchers rated every video with GQS, JAMA and Modified DISCERN; concordance coefficients 0.227/0.206/0.037, discrepancies resolved by consensus. No ground-truth accuracy coding.
rob.item6_quote: The JAMA Benchmark Criteria is a 4-point scale to determine the videos and resources' reliability and accuracy. The four criteria are: (1) authorship, (2) attribution, (3) disclosure, and (4) currency.
rob.item10_quote: Most of the videos had partially sufficient data (2 or 3 points on the JAMA scale) (69.5%, n = 116).
